analysis.one_liner: Replaces the income tax with a 17% flat tax and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The flat-tax bill had zero cosponsors, never got a hearing in the Senate Finance Committee, and died when the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would throw out the current tax code and replace it with a single 17% tax rate for both individuals and businesses. It would tax only wages, retirement payouts, and unemployment checks, while leaving investment income like capital gains, dividends, and interest untaxed at the individual level. It would also repeal the estate tax, every income tax credit, the alternative minimum tax, and key rules protecting workers' pensions.
analysis.who_benefits: High earners would see their top rate drop from 35% to 17%. Investors and heirs to large estates would benefit most of all: the bill's definition of taxable income counts only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation, so capital gains, dividends, and interest would escape individual tax entirely, and the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes would be repealed. Corporations and business owners would pay 17% instead of the 35% corporate rate, deducting the cost of inputs and wages. Employers with overfunded pension plans could pull the surplus out for themselves without paying the current 20% excise tax.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and large estates

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the progressive rate structure, whose top rate was 35%, with a single 17% rate on individual taxable income, so the largest percentage tax cuts go to the highest earners.

Redefines taxable income to cover only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation above the standard deduction — leaving capital gains, dividends, interest, and other investment income out of individual taxation altogether.
Repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes, eliminating the federal tax on very large inheritances for deaths after December 31, 2011.
Cuts the corporate tax to a 17% levy on business taxable income — gross receipts minus the cost of business inputs and cash wages — down from the 35% corporate rate.
Repeals the alternative minimum tax and all income tax credits.
Repeals the 20% excise tax on pension reversions and lets employers transfer excess defined-benefit pension assets back to themselves, owing only ordinary income tax on the withdrawal.
Repeals pension nondiscrimination rules, compensation and contribution limits, and minimum coverage requirements, so a company plan could legally concentrate benefits on its highest-paid executives.

analysis.who_pays: Working families would lose every income tax credit, including the Earned Income Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit, which currently put cash back in the paychecks of low- and moderate-wage workers — so many households would owe more than they do now even at the lower 17% rate. Wage earners in general would bear a larger share of the tax burden as investment income and inheritances go untaxed. Workers at companies with overfunded pensions could see surplus retirement money pulled out by their employers. The bill also repeals no spending, so the revenue lost to the rate cuts and estate-tax repeal would show up either as larger deficits or as pressure to cut programs later.

drawbacks.text: Repealing all income tax credits means eliminating the Earned Income Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit, which for many working households are worth more than the income tax they currently owe — a family could face a net tax increase despite the flat 17% rate.

Because taxable income would count only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation, income from investments — capital gains, dividends, interest, rents — would face no individual tax at all, shifting the tax burden onto people who work for a living.
Repealing the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes would end the only federal tax on multi-million-dollar inheritances.

Letting employers reclaim excess pension assets without the 20% excise tax, and repealing pension nondiscrimination and minimum-coverage rules, would weaken retirement security for rank-and-file workers.

Title II would lock in the flat structure: any future bill raising a rate, cutting the standard deduction, or adding any tax benefit would need a three-fifths vote in both chambers to even come up for consideration.

The bill raises new costs on some employers: tax-exempt organizations and federal, state, and local governments would owe a 17% tax on the value of fringe benefits such as health coverage they provide employees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The simplification is real — a postcard-sized return with one rate and one deduction would be genuinely easier than today's code, and repealing the alternative minimum tax would spare many households a confusing parallel calculation. But the design of the bill overwhelmingly favors people who live off investments and inheritances: it untaxes investment income at the individual level, repeals the estate tax, and pays for those cuts in part by taking away the Earned Income Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit from working families and by letting employers raid overfunded pensions. On balance, this is a large shift of the tax load away from concentrated wealth and onto wages.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Shelby introduced the SMART Act on April 14, 2011, delivering introductory remarks and proposing to replace the entire income tax code with a 17% flat tax.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day, and no other senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The Finance Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything, because nothing happened — but working families are better off that it died: they kept the Earned Income Tax Credit, the Child Tax Credit, and pension nondiscrimination rules that this bill would have repealed, and the wealthy households and corporations that stood to gain from the 17% rate, untaxed investment income, and estate-tax repeal simply stayed under the existing code.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Working families; the existing tax code stayed

for.name: Richard C. Shelby
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor, and was its only sponsor.

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Committee took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it never advanced.

against.name: Every other U.S. senator
against.what_they_did: Not one senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote and attracted zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split was ever tested; a Republican wrote it and a Democratic-controlled committee let it sit.

industries.note: The bill would cut the top individual rate from 35% to 17%, leave capital gains, dividends, and interest untaxed at the individual level, and repeal the estate and gift taxes. Its gains for concentrated wealth come directly from shifting the tax burden onto wages and working families.
A 17% tax on business taxable income replaces the 35% corporate rate, with wages and business inputs fully deductible. The revenue given up would have to be made up elsewhere or added to deficits.

industries.industry: Sponsors of overfunded defined-benefit pension plans
industries.note: Employers could transfer excess pension assets back to the company without the current 20% reversion excise tax, owing only income tax on the withdrawal — money that today is held in trust for workers.
These employers would owe a new 17% tax on the value of noncash fringe benefits like health insurance, pressuring nonprofits and governments to cut back employee benefits.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax advisory services
industries.note: A one-rate, one-deduction code with no credits or AMT would shrink the market for preparing and planning around complex returns — a cost to the industry that comes precisely from simplifying life for ordinary filers.
